a_rain_source.title: Rain source
a_rain_source.question: How much skill is lost when rain comes from a satellite instead of rain gauges, and does satellite rain add anything on top of gauge rain?

read_first_gains_1_day_ahead: Satellite rain, soil wetness and precipitable water of the issue day are UTC-day values: their day ends at 19:00 local standard time. The gauge-based rain of the issue day ends earlier: it matches satellite rain of the UTC day before (0.55) as well as of the same UTC day (0.59; median correlations). The UTC-day inputs therefore already hold rain that the gauge table books on the next day (correlation with next-day gauge rain: gauge-based rain (Daymet) itself 0.26; satellite rain (IMERG) 0.55; day-to-day change of top-layer soil wetness (MERRA-2) 0.49; precipitable water (MERRA-2) 0.30). A gain 1 day ahead can come from this later time stamp alone: it does not show that satellite rain is more accurate than rain gauges, or that soil storage or moisture in the air adds skill (see notes).

notes: LSTM settings: results/lstm_all.json, key 'config' (chosen there on the validation years of the main split); the number of updates is capped at 1000 and the patience at 5 checks to keep the script near 30 minutes on this laptop. 0 of 30 trainings had their best validation score within the last two checks before the cap, i.e. might have improved a little with more updates.

Experiment (a) uses its own satellite-era split (training 2000-10-01..2008-09-30, validation 2008-10-01..2010-09-30, test 2010-10-01..2014-09-30): 8 training years instead of 20, 4 test years instead of 9, and high-flow thresholds from ITS training years. Its numbers are NOT comparable with the main split (experiment (b), 04_lstm_all.py); only the differences inside the experiment mean something.

Equal data: inside an experiment all variants, the base included, read tables cropped to the same first day (data_start), so they are trained and scored on identical days (same first forecast day; coverage 1.0 in the validation and test years - asserted). The base of (b) therefore starts three months later than lstm_w / lstm_wq of 04_lstm_all.py and is not identical to them.

Seeds: 2 per variant. 'difference' = mean over the seeds of the variant minus mean over the seeds of the base, for the median test NSE of the 12 basins (single trainings, not the seed average). difference_min / max = every seed of the variant against every seed of the base. seed_noise = how much two trainings of the SAME model differ on average (mean absolute difference between seeds, averaged over the variants of the experiment and input set). larger_than_seed_noise is true only when the difference is more than twice the seed noise AND all seed pairs agree in sign. With 2 seeds the sign rule alone would be met by chance in 1 in 3 comparisons, which is why the second condition is added. A simulation with random seed noise and no real difference (seed_noise_rule) makes the full rule fire in 10% / 8% of comparisons (3 variants in the noise estimate / 4 variants in the noise estimate); 33 comparisons of the median NSE are made here without correction, so about 3 'true' are expected by chance alone: a single 'true' is weak evidence, a pattern over leads and input sets counts for more.

n_basins_improved, the per-basin scores under 'test' and the saved prediction sets use the seed-average forecast (day-by-day mean of the seeds) of each variant. Single basins are less stable than the median of the 12: between two trainings of the same model the test NSE of one basin 1 day ahead differs by 0.02 in the median and by up to 0.28 (Charlie Creek, FL, gauge-based rain (Daymet), past weather; seed_noise_single_basin). n_basins_improved counts every basin with a higher NSE, however small the gain, so only counts near 0 or near 12 carry weight, and a gain can sit in a few basins (per-basin scores: experiments, variants, sets, test, basins).

The test years chose nothing: settings come from the validation years of the main split, every stopping point from the validation years of the experiment's own split, and no variant was selected here.

Satellite rain = GPM IMERG as served by NASA POWER, averaged over each basin. From 2001 it is the Final Run, which is corrected with monthly rain-gauge analyses and published about 3.5 months late; the run before 2001 is not stated by the source. The experiment therefore shows the best case for satellite rain, not what a real-time warning system would have (Early/Late runs, not tested).

The IMERG day is the UTC day, which ends at 19:00 local standard time (18:00 for Leaf River): the value of day t is complete at the issue time (end of local day t), so nothing from after the issue time is used (flood.fit also checks that the network cannot read later days). The Daymet day is a different one: its rain of day d matches the UTC days d-1 and d about equally well and the UTC day d+1 hardly at all (median correlations 0.55, 0.59, 0.05; results/satellite_data.json), as if it held the 24 hours up to the morning of day d. Satellite rain of issue day t therefore includes rain that fell later on day t (up to 19:00) and that Daymet books on day t+1. A gain from satellite rain can come from this later day boundary as well as from the rain amounts; this experiment cannot separate the two, and a loss with 'satellite instead of gauge' is the net of worse amounts and a later boundary.

The same holds for the MERRA-2 inputs, which are UTC-day values too. What each input of issue day d already tells about the rain that Daymet books on day d+1 (median correlation over the basins, training years of (a); what_inputs_know_about_next_daymet_day): gauge-based rain (Daymet) itself 0.26; satellite rain (IMERG) 0.55; day-to-day change of top-layer soil wetness (MERRA-2) 0.49; precipitable water (MERRA-2) 0.30. An input that scores higher here than Daymet rain itself carries rain information the base model does not have at issue time. A gain 1 day ahead from satellite rain, soil wetness or precipitable water is therefore at least partly a gain from a later observation time, not proof that the quantity itself (soil storage, moisture in the air) adds skill. If this reading of the Daymet day is right, part of what 04_lstm_all.py reports as the value of a 'perfect weather forecast' 1 day ahead is also rain that had already fallen at issue time.

Daymet does not measure sunlight; it estimates it from the daily temperature range and from whether rain was reported. In these basins its sunlight is on average 35% lower on days with at least 1 mm of gauge-based rain than on drier days of the same calendar month (median of 12 basins, training years of (a)). A model without gauge rain can read rain days from it, so the variant 'imerg_nosun' removes it (past weather only). Temperature and humidity are still Daymet's, i.e. station-based: a fully gauge-free input set was not tested.

Soil wetness (GWETTOP, GWETROOT) and precipitable water (TQV) are MERRA-2 reanalysis values of the one 0.5 x 0.625 degree cell that holds the basin centroid: a weather model that assimilates satellite and other observations, not a direct satellite retrieval, and published weeks after the fact. Its rain over land is corrected with rain-gauge analyses and drives the land model that computes the soil wetness (results/satellite_data.json, notes and documentation), so soil wetness is a modelled quantity and not independent of rain gauges; like the IMERG Final Run, a product computed after the fact can carry corrections that rest on observations made after the day it describes. Precipitable water is the quantity GNSS receivers measure; no GNSS data were used.

Warning scores are pooled over the 12 basins; high flow = above the basin's 95th percentile of the training years of the split; onset = forecasts issued while the river was still at or below that level. The test years of experiment (a) hold 335 onset days (1 day ahead, all basins) against 611 in experiment (b), so the warning scores of (a) are the noisier ones.
